stem:
This statement is true:
"Ella passed the exam and Fe passed the exam."

Which must be true?
choices: Ella passed, but Fe did not.
Fe passed, but Ella did not.
At least one of them failed.
hints: An "and" statement joins two smaller statements. Think about when the whole thing can be true.
Split it: part 1 is "Ella passed"; part 2 is "Fe passed".
An "and" statement is true only when both parts are true. Use that to decide what each part must be, then pick the choice that matches.

solution.methodName: Mark each part true or false, then combine

steps.action: Split the statement into its two parts: "Ella passed" and "Fe passed".
An "and" statement is true only when both parts are true.
steps.why: If either part were false, the whole "and" statement would be false. Think of a notice that says "Bring an ID and a photo": you must bring both.

steps.action: The statement is true, so both parts are true: Ella passed and Fe passed.
"Ella passed, but Fe did not" and "Fe passed, but Ella did not" each make one part false, so they cannot be true here.
"At least one of them failed" also makes a part false, so it is false.
The answer is "Both Ella and Fe passed."

If Fe did not pass, the part "Fe passed" would be false, and the whole "and" statement would be false. But we are told it is true.
If Ella did not pass, the part "Ella passed" would be false, and the whole "and" statement would be false. But we are told it is true.
This would make at least one part false. A true "and" statement means neither of them failed.
